title: Rolling Galleries: How Nairobi's Matatus Became Art on Wheels
excerpt: Spray-painted portraits, nine screens and bass you can feel in your ribs: the nganya is Nairobi's loudest art form, and it runs to a timetable. Sort of.
content:
Stand at a stage in the CBD at rush hour and you will see it coming before you hear it. Then you hear it. A 33-seater wrapped in airbrushed portraits, LED strips chasing each other along the roofline, a bass line that rattles the windows of the bank across the road. A conductor hangs from the door, shouting a destination you can barely make out over the music. Welcome to the nganya, Nairobi's mobile art gallery, nightclub and commuter service in one.

Other cities have buses. Nairobi has rolling statements. Here is how a humble minibus turned into one of the most distinctive pieces of street culture anywhere in the world.

Thirty cents and a pickup

The matatu began in the 1950s in Eastlands, where colonial-era restrictions had left Africans with very little public transport. Enterprising owners filled the gap with whatever vehicles they could get, and the trade grew quickly after independence. The name is usually traced to the fare: three ten-cent coins, or thirty cents, with the Gikuyu word for "three" giving us "matatu". A 1973 presidential decree allowed the vehicles to carry fare-paying passengers without a full transport licence, and the floodgates opened.

Through the 1980s and 1990s the 14-seater Nissan minibus became so common that people still call any small matatu "a Nissan", even though Toyota vans long ago took over most of the fleet. Today the city's matatus run on numbered routes set by the authorities, crewed by a driver and a conductor, and organised into saccos that own or manage the vehicles.

From paint job to nganya

Decoration arrived early, but the full-blown art movement is a product of competition. On a crowded route, the vehicle that looks and sounds best fills first. So owners began spending serious money on their buses, and the "nganya" (also called a "manyanga") was born: a matatu built to be seen.

A proper nganya starts life as a bare chassis. A custom body is built, then the interior is fitted with seats, a sound system, screens, CCTV and lighting, and finally the outside is covered in stickers or airbrushed art. Reports from the trade put the customisation bill at roughly KSh 2 million to KSh 6.5 million, and the whole process can take three to eight months. One graffiti artist interviewed by The Standard put the price of a used 33-seater at around KSh 2.5 million and a new one at KSh 7–15 million before any of the fun begins. A personalised number plate on its own can reportedly run to a million shillings.

What goes on the outside

The artwork is where the personality lives. Expect portraits of footballers, musicians and film characters, anime murals, religious imagery, slogans in Sheng and English, and themes that run from bumper to bumper. In June 2025, for example, a nganya called Detroit 313 launched on the Ongata Rongai route wrapped in Detroit Lions graffiti. Names matter as much as paint: Dethrone, B613, Code, Dynasty, Subzero, Night Nurse, Boom Box, Batman, Ambush, Matrix Damager and Scar are among the buses that have become famous in their own right.

What goes on the inside

Step aboard and the experience changes again. The best nganyas run imported sound systems with speakers placed for a surround-sound effect, multiple screens playing music videos (nine screens in the Detroit 313's case), strobe lighting and branded decals. Some now even have live DJs or a "TikTok corner" where passengers film content. It is not unusual for an artist to premiere a song on the matatu circuit before it trends online, which tells you how much influence these vehicles have over what Nairobi listens to.

The crews

A nganya is a team effort. The owner funds it, the sacco manages it, the artists and fabricators build it, and the crew brings it to life every day. The driver is the star; the conductor, or "makanga", is the hype man, fare collector and lookout rolled into one, using a distinctive vocabulary of whistles, taps on the bodywork and shouted calls. Touts at the stage, sometimes called "kamagera", work the crowds to fill seats.

The economics are tough. A driver quoted by Citizen Digital reported earnings of around KSh 6,000–10,000 a day, while other estimates put a matatu's daily takings between KSh 5,000 and KSh 15,000. When you have spent millions on a bus, every seat counts, and that pressure explains a great deal about how nganyas are driven.

Women are increasingly part of the story too, as conductors and drivers, although they report a tough working environment.

The law and the backlash

Matatu culture has always had a complicated relationship with authority. In 2004 the government introduced sweeping road-safety rules that made seat belts compulsory, imposed speed governors and banned much of the art and loud music. For a while the buses went plain. The rules were relaxed about a decade later and the paint came back, brighter than ever.

The National Transport and Safety Authority (NTSA) still points out that matatus are involved in a disproportionate share of crashes, citing speeding, aggressive lane changes, worn brakes and unauthorised modifications. Noise and overloading are regular targets of crackdowns. Plenty of commuters will tell you they love the music and the speed; plenty of others will tell you they would happily trade both for an open window and a calmer ride. Both groups are right.

A nganya is part public transport, part music video and part competitive sport. That is why it is impossible to ignore.

Where to see the best of it

If you want to appreciate the art without riding at 7am, here are a few pointers:

  • The CBD stages. Archives and the stages around Moi Avenue and Tom Mboya Street in the evening rush are where the big names line up.
  • The famous routes. Eastlands estates and the Ongata Rongai route have long been known for competitive nganyas.
  • Launch nights and awards. New nganyas are often unveiled with parties, and competitions such as the Beba Awards celebrate the best-revamped buses. Watch social media for dates.
  • Ask first. Crews are usually proud to show off their work, but always ask before you climb in to photograph an interior, and do not block a stage when the bus needs to load.

Why it matters

Strip away the volume and the nganya is something remarkable: a fully home-grown, commercially funded art movement that tours the city every day, free to look at. It gives work to painters, welders, upholsterers, sound engineers and coders. It launches songs and trends. It reflects whatever Nairobi is obsessed with this month, from a football club to a cartoon.

Car people sometimes forget that culture is not only about horsepower. The nganya is our most visible proof that Kenyans customise vehicles with as much passion as anyone on earth. It just happens to stop at your stage, take your fifty bob and play you the next big hit on the way home.

title: Blue, Gold and Boxer Rumble: Why Kenya Fell for the Subaru
excerpt: From Safari Rally glory to Sunday drag strips, the Subaru Impreza became a Kenyan obsession. We trace the love affair, burble and all.
content:
Every Kenyan knows the sound. A slightly off-beat, lumpy burble from a car that looks perfectly ordinary until you notice the bonnet scoop, the gold wheels and the exhaust tip the size of a sufuria. Somewhere on Mombasa Road, a Subaru is clearing its throat.

No other performance brand has worked its way into Kenyan popular culture quite like Subaru. It has its own stereotypes, its own memes and its own clubs, and its owners are some of the most devoted car people in the country. So how did a mid-sized Japanese company best known abroad for sensible four-wheel-drive estates become the default dream car of a generation of young Kenyans?

It started in the mud

The short answer is the Safari Rally. In the 1990s the Safari was a round of the World Rally Championship, and it was the toughest event on the calendar. Kenyans lined the roads in their thousands to watch the world's best drivers attack rough tracks around Nairobi, Naivasha and beyond.

Subaru's blue cars with their yellow stars became a fixture. Colin McRae and Nicky Grist won the 1997 Safari in the Subaru Impreza WRC97, and Richard Burns and Robert Reid followed up in 2000 in the Impreza WRC00. Just as importantly, a Kenyan was in the team: Patrick Njiru, born in Kevote, Embu, drove for the Subaru World Rally Team on the Safari across the 1980s and 1990s. Seeing a local hero in works blue did a great deal for the brand's standing at home.

When the WRC left Kenya after 2002, the Safari carried on as a regional event, and Subarus kept winning. Carl Tundo and Tim Jessop won in an Impreza in 2004, Conrad Rautenbach and Peter Marsh won in an Impreza N10 in 2007, and Tapio Laukkanen and Gavin Laurence won in an Impreza WRX STI in 2017. The rivalry with the Mitsubishi Lancer Evolution, which won many of the in-between years, became the Kenyan version of a football derby.

The road car that made the dream affordable

Rally success sells cars only if people can buy something similar. Here Subaru had a huge advantage: the Japanese used-car pipeline. Because Kenya imports the overwhelming majority of its used vehicles from Japan, second-hand Imprezas, WRXs, Legacys and Foresters landed in Mombasa in large numbers. A turbocharged, four-wheel-drive saloon that looked like the rally car was suddenly within reach of a young professional.

The ingredients suited Kenyan roads perfectly:

  • Symmetrical all-wheel drive gave grip on wet murram and on Nairobi roads slick with the first rains.
  • The boxer engine sits low in the car, which helps handling, and produces that unmistakable sound, especially the older EJ-series units with unequal-length headers.
  • Turbocharging made the WRX properly quick for the money, and very responsive to tuning.
  • Practicality. Under the attitude, an Impreza is a usable family saloon or estate.

The "Subaru boy" and other legends

With popularity came a reputation. The stereotype of the young, loud, fast-driving "Subaru boy" became a running joke in Kenyan media, complete with tales of modified exhausts, cars that cost more than the owner's rent several times over, and weekend runs to Naivasha. Like all stereotypes it is unfair to most owners, but it also says something about how visible the cars became.

The joke does not stop women either. The Subie Queens Motoring Club was founded on 24 March 2016 with 11 members after a group of women decided to start their own space for Subaru owners. It went on to run car clinics, charity drives and road-safety work, with branches in Kisumu, Mombasa, Eldoret, Nakuru, Embu and Kisii.

Clubs, meets and drag strips

Kenya's Subaru community is organised and busy. The Subaru Owners Club has run annual time trials and car festivals with timed runs and drag strips, and there are separate groups for particular models such as the Legacy and Forester. Most of the activity is coordinated on social media and WhatsApp, with Sunday morning meets and convoys to big events.

At the sharp end, Nairobi now has Subarus that would embarrass a supercar. Top Gear visited Rupal Racing, the workshop run by brothers Karan and Simar Rupal in Nairobi's industrial area, where most of the cars on the floor are Imprezas. Karan's own first-generation GC8 Impreza has a fully built 2.5-litre EJ25 engine that he estimates makes about 900bhp on E85. Kenya has no purpose-built drag strip, so drag events are held on airstrips and on public roads closed with permits; venues such as Masinga Dam Airstrip in Machakos County and Nyaribo Airstrip in Nyeri County have hosted drag racing and gymkhana.

The Safari still pulls them in

Since the Safari returned to the WRC in 2021, with its stages around Naivasha, it has become the biggest Subaru meet in the country in all but name. Fans drive up from all over Kenya, and the roads and campsites around Naivasha fill with Imprezas, Foresters and Legacys. The cars on the stages are now Toyotas, Hyundais and Fords, but in the spectator car parks, Subaru blue is still the colour of the weekend.

Is the love affair cooling?

There are pressures. Fuel is expensive, insurers are wary of modified cars, and Kenya's import rules now only admit vehicles first registered within the last eight years, which means the classic GC8 and GD-generation cars have to be found locally. Subaru also ended the EJ-engined STI and the current WRX uses a newer 2.4-litre engine with a different, smoother voice.

Yet the scene keeps renewing itself. Newer WRXs, Levorgs and Foresters with turbo engines are arriving, older cars are being restored rather than scrapped, and every new driver who hears that burble at a petrol station seems to catch the bug.

Kenya did not fall for the Subaru because of an advert. It fell for it on the roadside, covered in Safari dust, watching a blue car go past sideways.

Joining in: a few tips

  • Buy on condition, not on looks. A tidy standard car is worth more than a loud one with a mystery tune.
  • Keep up with oil changes. Boxer engines, especially turbo ones, reward frequent, quality oil changes and punish neglect.
  • Protect the underside. A sump guard is a wise buy on Kenyan roads.
  • Find your people. Owners' clubs are the fastest route to a trusted mechanic and honest advice.
  • Save the speed for the strip. Organised events exist precisely so the fun stays off public roads.

title: Ten Legends of the Safari: The Cars That Conquered Kenya
excerpt: From the Datsun 240Z to the hybrid GR Yaris, these are the ten cars that tamed the toughest rally on earth, checked against the record books.
content:
The Safari Rally has broken more cars than any other event in the sport's history. Rocks the size of footballs, bull dust that swallows whole cars, rivers that rise in an afternoon and, in the old days, thousands of kilometres of open road between start and finish. To win here you needed a fast driver, a brave co-driver and, above all, a car that refused to die.

Plenty of famous machines came to Kenya and left on a lorry. These ten did not. Every result below has been checked against the Safari's official roll of honour.

1. Datsun 240Z (1971, 1973)

A sports car on the Safari sounds absurd, yet the 240Z was perfect for it. Its 2.4-litre straight-six was strong and simple, and the long-legged chassis coped with endless high-speed murram. Edgar Herrmann and Hans Schüller won in 1971, a year after taking the 1970 event in a Datsun 1600 SSS, and Shekhar Mehta with Lofty Drews won in a 240Z in 1973. It cemented Datsun as the Safari's great Japanese pioneer, long before rallying became a Japanese-dominated sport.

2. Ford Escort RS1600 and RS1800 (1972, 1977)

The Escort was the darling of British forests, but its Safari win in 1972 was historic: Hannu Mikkola and Gunnar Palm became the first crew from outside East Africa to win the event. Five years later Björn Waldegård and Hans Thorszelius did it again in the RS1800. Light, rear-wheel drive and endlessly fixable, the Escort was proof that the Safari could be won with agility as well as brute strength.

3. Peugeot 504 (1975, 1978)

No list of Safari heroes is complete without Peugeot. The 404 had already won four times in the 1960s (1963, 1966, 1967 and 1968), and its successor kept the tradition alive. Ove Andersson and Arne Hertz won in a 504 saloon in 1975, and Jean-Pierre Nicolas and Jean-Claude Lefèbvre won in the 504 V6 Coupé in 1978. The 504's soft, long-travel suspension and toughness made it a legend on the stages and, just as importantly, on Kenyan roads, where it became the country's signature saloon.

4. Datsun 160J and Nissan Violet GT (1979–1982)

Shekhar Mehta holds the record for most Safari wins, with five, and four of them came in a row with Mike Doughty alongside: 1979 and 1980 in the Datsun 160J, then 1981 and 1982 in the Nissan Violet GT, essentially the same car under its Japanese name. It was not the fastest car of the era, but it was relentlessly reliable and superbly prepared, which on the Safari matters more than anything.

5. Toyota Celica Twin-Cam Turbo (1984, 1985, 1986)

In the age of four-wheel-drive Group B monsters, a rear-wheel-drive Celica should not have stood a chance. Instead the Twin-Cam Turbo, known as the TCT, won three Safaris on the trot: Björn Waldegård and Hans Thorszelius in 1984, Juha Kankkunen and Fred Gallagher in 1985, and Waldegård and Gallagher in 1986. Toyota had built a car specifically for African rallying, prioritising strength over outright speed, and it paid off handsomely.

6. Lancia Delta HF Integrale (1988, 1989, 1991)

Lancia had come close on the Safari before, but the Delta finally cracked it. Miki Biasion and Tiziano Siviero won back-to-back in 1988 and 1989, and Juha Kankkunen and Juha Piironen added a third win in 1991. The turbocharged, four-wheel-drive Delta was the dominant rally car of its generation, and these wins proved it could survive Kenya as well as it could win in Europe.

7. Toyota Celica GT-Four (1990, 1992–1995)

If one car owns the Safari's modern history, it is this one. Björn Waldegård won his fourth Safari in the GT-Four in 1990, and the later Celica Turbo 4WD then won four years running: Carlos Sainz and Luis Moya in 1992, Kankkunen and Piironen in 1993, Kenya's own Ian Duncan with David Williamson in 1994, and Yoshio Fujimoto with Arne Hertz in 1995, the first Japanese driver to win the Safari. Ian Duncan's victory remains one of the proudest moments in Kenyan motorsport.

A word on Kenyan winners

Local crews have always punched above their weight here. Joginder Singh, the "Flying Sikh", won three times (1965 in a Volvo PV544, then 1974 and 1976 in a Mitsubishi Lancer 1600 GSR), Shekhar Mehta won five, and after the Safari left the world championship, Kenyan drivers such as Carl Tundo, Baldev Chager and Jaspreet Singh Chatthe dominated the regional era.

8. Subaru Impreza WRC (1997, 2000)

The car that launched a thousand Kenyan Subaru fan clubs. Colin McRae and Nicky Grist won in the Impreza WRC97 in 1997, the first year of the World Rally Car regulations, and Richard Burns and Robert Reid won in the Impreza WRC00 in 2000. The blue-and-yellow Impreza looked spectacular in the dust, and its success fed directly into the Subaru culture that still dominates Kenyan car meets.

9. Mitsubishi Lancer Evolution (1996, 2001 and the regional era)

Mitsubishi's Safari story runs from Joginder Singh's Lancer 1600 GSR wins in the 1970s to the Evolution era. Tommi Mäkinen and Seppo Harjanne won in a Lancer Evo III in 1996, Richard Burns won in the closely related Carisma GT in 1998, and Mäkinen returned to win in the Evo 6.5 in 2001 with Risto Mannisenmäki. Then, after the Safari dropped off the WRC calendar, the Evo became the car to have in the regional championship, with Evo VI, VII, IX and X models winning the event again and again between 2003 and 2019.

10. Toyota GR Yaris Rally1 (2022–2026)

When the Safari returned to the World Rally Championship in 2021, Sébastien Ogier and Julien Ingrassia won in the Yaris WRC. Then came the hybrid era, and Toyota's GR Yaris Rally1 has won every Safari since. In 2022 Kalle Rovanperä and Jonne Halttunen led a historic Toyota one-two-three-four. Ogier (with Vincent Landais) won in 2023, Rovanperä again in 2024, Elfyn Evans and Scott Martin in 2025, and in March 2026 Takamoto Katsuta and Aaron Johnston took a richly deserved maiden WRC victory after Toyota lost three cars on the Saturday.

That run takes Toyota to 14 Safari wins, from the first Celica TCT to the latest Yaris, making it one of the two most successful manufacturers in the event's history alongside Mitsubishi.

Honourable mentions

  • Opel Ascona 400, which carried Ari Vatanen and Terry Harryman to victory in 1983.
  • Audi 200 Quattro, an unlikely big-saloon winner for Hannu Mikkola and Arne Hertz in 1987.
  • Ford Focus WRC, which gave Colin McRae two more Safari wins, in 1999 and 2002.
  • Volkswagen Beetle, winner of the very first event in 1953 and several more in the 1950s and 1960s.
On the Safari, the fastest car rarely wins. The car that is still running on Sunday does.

title: Rhino Charge Explained: Kenya's Gloriously Mad Off-Road Fundraiser
excerpt: Thirteen checkpoints, ten hours, no roads and every metre counted by GPS. Here is how the Rhino Charge works, and where its record millions go.
content:
Imagine a motor race where the fastest car does not win, where you are penalised for speeding, and where the main event is a fundraising drive. Then add a remote patch of Kenyan bush, a map, a winch cable and a co-driver hanging off the side of the car shouting directions through an acacia thicket. That is the Rhino Charge, and there is nothing else quite like it.

Since 1989 it has raised billions of shillings to protect Kenya's mountain forests. In 2026 it raised more than ever. Here is how it all works.

How it began

The Rhino Charge was conceived in Nairobi to raise money for an electric fence around the Aberdare range, a project run by the Rhino Ark charitable trust, which had been set up in 1988. The first event was held on 4 February 1989. Thirty-one vehicles entered, the winner was Travers Allison in a Suzuki, and the day raised KSh 250,000.

The Aberdare fence that money helped start was completed in 2009 and stretches about 400 km. Rhino Ark has since taken on Mount Kenya, Mau Eburu and other "water towers", the forests that feed the rivers most Kenyans depend on. By 2025 the organisation said the event had contributed to some 805 km of electric fence across mountain forest ecosystems, and total funds raised over the years had passed KSh 2.4 billion.

The basic idea

The format is beautifully simple. Each team gets a map of an area of roughly 100 square kilometres of rough country and the GPS coordinates of 13 checkpoints, traditionally called guard posts. Teams choose their own route between them. The aim is to visit as many checkpoints as possible within the time allowed and return to finish, while covering the shortest distance.

  • The winner is the team that visits the most checkpoints; ties are broken by the shortest distance, measured by GPS tracker, and then by time.
  • The clock runs for about ten hours, from a mass start at 07:30 to the close of checkpoints in the late afternoon.
  • The start is drawn at random, so every car begins at a different checkpoint, convoyed there before dawn.
  • The venue changes every year and is kept under wraps until the last moment, so local knowledge counts for little.

The shortest-distance rule is the clever bit. It rewards teams that go straight over a ridge or through a gully rather than around it, and that is why Rhino Charge cars spend so much of the day on their winches.

The gauntlet

Modern rules add a Compulsory Gauntlet: a set of designated checkpoint gates that every entrant must pass through before visiting the other checkpoints. It is a test of skill in its own right, and the Gauntlet has its own results table. There are further awards for the fastest "tiger lines" and an overall all-rounder prize, the Victor Ludorum.

The rules that keep it honest

The organisers are serious about the environment and safety, and the penalties show it. Under the current regulations:

  • Exceeding 40 km/h for 12 seconds adds 100 m to your distance, and repeated offences cost checkpoints.
  • Driving along marked roads is limited, with distance penalties and checkpoint deductions for overuse.
  • Entering a no-go zone adds a kilometre to your distance.
  • Oversized tyres or breaching weight limits cost a checkpoint.
  • External assistance, unsafe driving or blocking other cars can bring penalties or disqualification.

The cars

Rhino Charge machines range from barely modified family 4x4s to purpose-built spaceframe specials that look like something from a film set. Entries are capped at 65 cars to limit the impact on the land, and there are three main classes, defined mainly by modifications and tyre size:

ClassMax tyre diameterWinches
Super-Modified1,016 mmUp to two, no hydraulic PTO winches
Modified939.8 mmUp to two
Unmodified863.6 mmTwo low-profile electric winches only

All vehicles must be registered and insured, weigh between 1,000 kg and 3,500 kg, and carry a roll cage, fire extinguishers, approved helmets, harnesses and drinking water. In 2025 the event saw its first locally assembled electric car take part, a sign of how the engineering is evolving.

There is also the Classic Charge, a shorter event with up to ten places, which finishes earlier in the afternoon.

In the field you will see heavily modified Land Rovers, Toyotas and Suzukis, and bespoke machines built in Kenyan workshops. Each team has a driver and a crew of "runners" who sprint ahead to find a line, guide the car and rig the winch. It is exhausting, and it is a team sport in every sense.

The money

Entry is not cheap, because that is the point. Under the 2027 rules, the minimum sponsorship pledge for a full entry starts at KSh 2 million when entries open and steps down to KSh 750,000 later in the window, plus a non-refundable KSh 100,000 early sponsorship. Teams raise this from companies, friends and online campaigns, and the biggest fundraisers compete as fiercely off the course as on it. The David Schaeffer Trophy goes to the team with the highest cash sponsorship.

Rhino Charge 2026: a record year

The 37th Rhino Charge was held at Ngilai Community Conservancy in Samburu County, with the full field of 65 cars. It raised KSh 365 million, the highest total in the event's history and up from KSh 269 million at Saimo-Soi in Baringo North in 2025.

  • Overall winner: Team Huzi, Car 33, led by Oliver Outram in the Super-Modified class, visited all 13 checkpoints over a course of about 27 km.
  • Top fundraiser: Adil Khawaja's Car 44 raised KSh 216 million, making him the top fundraiser for the fourth year running.
  • Community dividend: Rhino Ark handed over KSh 9.1 million for community projects in Ngilai.

The 2027 event is scheduled for Saturday 29 May 2027.

Where the money goes

Funds go to Rhino Ark's work protecting Kenya's mountain forest ecosystems: building and maintaining electric fences, repairing damage, surveillance, and supporting communities who live alongside the fences with projects such as tree nurseries, water schemes and fire-fighting equipment. The fences reduce human-wildlife conflict, protect farms from crop-raiding elephants and help stop illegal logging and charcoal burning. Because Charge money is flexible, Rhino Ark can use it to keep existing projects running, which is often the hardest kind of funding to find.

The Rhino Charge turns the urge to drive somewhere ridiculous into fences, forests and water for millions of Kenyans. Few motorsport events can say that.

Want to go?

Spectator access is controlled by the organisers, so follow Rhino Charge's official channels well in advance for details. Bring your own water, food and patience, respect the host community, and stay well back from cars on the move: a winch cable under tension is no place for a selfie.

title: The Great Kenyan Driving Roads: Escarpments, Tea and Kerio Valley Hairpins
excerpt: Kenya hides some of Africa's best driving roads behind its traffic jams. Here are our favourites, from the Rift Valley plunge to the Kerio Valley switchbacks, plus how to drive them well.
content:
Ask a Kenyan driver about roads and you will usually hear about potholes, speed bumps and lorries. Fair enough. But get out of Nairobi early on a Sunday and you discover something else entirely: escarpments that fall a kilometre in a few minutes, tea estates folded over hills like green corduroy, and valley roads where every corner is a viewpoint.

These are our favourite drives for people who actually enjoy driving. None of them is a racetrack. All of them are spectacular.

1. The Rift Valley escarpment via Mai Mahiu

Route: Nairobi to Naivasha via the old escarpment road, about 95 km.

This is the classic. Leave the city through Limuru and suddenly the earth falls away: the Great Rift Valley opens up beneath you, with Mount Longonot's crater on the horizon. Pull in at the viewpoints along the edge, including the popular Mathore viewpoint, then wind your way down the escarpment towards Mai Mahiu.

Near the bottom, look out for the tiny chapel built by Italian prisoners of war, completed towards the end of 1942 and now a gazetted national monument. It is one of the smallest churches you will ever see and a lovely spot to stop.

Watch out for: heavy lorries crawling up and down, and impatient overtakers. Use lower gears on the descent rather than cooking your brakes.

2. Ngong Hills to Lake Magadi

Route: Nairobi via Ngong and Kiserian to Lake Magadi, about 112 km.

The Magadi road is a tremendous descent into the floor of the Rift, from the cool green ridge of the Ngong Hills into acacia country and finally to the pink-and-white soda flats of Lake Magadi, home to flamingos. It gets hot down there, so it feels like driving into another country in the space of an hour. Olepolos is a well-known nyama choma stop on the way.

Watch out for: livestock on the road, and the heat. Carry plenty of water and keep an eye on your temperature gauge on the climb home.

3. Nyeri, Nanyuki and the Timau wheat country

Route: Nyeri – Kiganjo – Nanyuki – Timau, with optional extension to Isiolo or Meru.

The winding stretch out of Nyeri towards Kiganjo is a joy, with sweeping bends through farmland and views of the Aberdares on one side and Mount Kenya on the other. Stop for the obligatory photo at the equator sign before Nanyuki, then continue north-east to Timau, where the road opens into vast wheat fields with the mountain looming over them. After the rains, the colours are unreal.

Watch out for: early morning mist and cold. Yes, cold.

4. Nakuru to Nyahururu

A quieter alternative with farmland and forest, climbing towards Nyahururu and Thomson's Falls. Combine it with the Nyeri run for a proper loop through the central highlands. The road through the Nyandarua farmland is gorgeous at sunset.

5. The Kericho tea roads

Route: Nakuru – Londiani – Kericho, then onwards to Kisumu or along the estate roads.

Kericho is Kenya's tea capital, and driving through it is like driving through a perfectly trimmed garden. The road winds through the Mau Forest and endless tea estates, with tight corners after the climb and frequent rain to keep things interesting. Look out for Nyaru's "World's End" viewpoint in the western highlands. Stock up on snacks in Kericho town before heading west.

Watch out for: slippery surfaces after rain, tea lorries and pickers walking along the verges.

6. Kabarnet to Iten across the Kerio Valley

Route: Kabarnet – Chebloch – Iten on the C51, part of the Kabarnet–Eldoret road (about 90 km in all).

If you only drive one road on this list, make it this one. Leaving Kabarnet, the road plunges into the Kerio Valley, dropping roughly 1,000 metres in not much more than the same horizontal distance. You cross the Kerio River at Chebloch Gorge, then climb the Tambach escarpment on the far side through a series of switchbacks that feel like an Alpine pass dropped into the tropics.

At the top, the Iten View Point, about 500 m beyond Iten towards Kabarnet, gives you a view down to the Kerio River roughly 1,000 m below, with the Tugen Hills running parallel to the Keiyo escarpment. This is the home of Kenya's champion runners, so do not be surprised to share the road with athletes on their morning training run.

Watch out for: sharp, steep bends with rockfall, runners and cyclists, and brakes overheating on the long descents. Some roads off the escarpment in Elgeyo Marakwet have a reputation as genuinely dangerous, so treat them with respect.

7. Isiolo to Marsabit

Once a multi-day expedition for lorries only, the road north from Isiolo is now tarmac and can be driven in a long day. It is the gateway to northern Kenya: huge skies, hills rising out of the desert, wildlife and very few other vehicles. It is a road for big-hearted touring rather than corners, but the sense of space is extraordinary.

Watch out for: long gaps between fuel stations and help. Fill up whenever you can, and check local security advice.

8. Nairobi to Mombasa (the honest entry)

Every Kenyan should drive the Mombasa road at least once, for the Tsavo landscapes, the views of the railway and, on a clear day, Kilimanjaro. But it is not a driver's road. It is a lorry corridor, and overtaking on it demands patience and discipline. Leave early, take breaks and save your enthusiasm for the coast roads at the other end.

At a glance

DriveBest forMain hazard
Mai Mahiu escarpmentRift Valley viewsLorries
Ngong – MagadiA dramatic descentHeat, livestock
Nyeri – Nanyuki – TimauFlowing bends, Mt KenyaMist
Kericho tea roadsScenery and cornersWet surfaces
Kabarnet – ItenHairpins and dramaSteep bends, rockfall
Isiolo – MarsabitBig-sky touringRemoteness

How to enjoy these roads properly

  • Go early. A 6am start beats the traffic, the lorries and the heat, and the light is better for photographs.
  • Drive in daylight. Unlit roads, animals, pedestrians and unmarked obstacles make night driving a bad idea outside town.
  • Respect the limits. Speed checks are common, and villages appear quickly. The joy of these roads is in the flow, not the top speed.
  • Use engine braking. On long descents, select a lower gear and let the engine do the work. Brake fade on an escarpment is terrifying.
  • Check your car. Tyres (including the spare), brake pads, fluids and wipers. Carry a jack, a wheel brace you know fits, a torch, water and a phone charger.
  • Expect the unexpected. Goats, cattle, boda bodas, children walking to school and overtaking lorries can appear round any bend.
  • Fuel up. Outside the main towns, stations can be far apart.
  • Be a good guest. Buy lunch locally, park considerately and keep your music and revs down through villages.
The best Kenyan driving roads are not about going fast. They are about sunrise on an escarpment, a perfect sequence of bends and a view that makes you pull over and just stare.

title: Made in Japan, Loved in Kenya: Inside the JDM Scene
excerpt: Nine out of ten used cars on our roads came from Japan. Here is why, what the eight-year rule means, and how a generation of Kenyans turned Japanese imports into a culture.
content:
Stand by any Kenyan road for five minutes and count the cars. Probox, Vitz, Fielder, Note, Demio, Forester, Harrier, Land Cruiser, Probox again. The vast majority were built for Japanese roads, sold to Japanese owners and then shipped across the Indian Ocean to start a second, much harder life here.

Kenya is one of the great used-car markets of the world, and Japan is its supplier. That relationship has shaped not just what we drive, but how we tune, talk about and celebrate cars.

The numbers

The scale is remarkable. In the 12 months to June 2023, Kenya imported 62,495 used vehicles, and 58,972 of them came from Japan, about 94 per cent. The next largest sources were the United Kingdom, with 1,921 units (mostly European brands), and Thailand with 1,061, mainly pickups.

Why Japan? Several things line up:

  • Right-hand drive. Kenya drives on the left, and Japan builds right-hand-drive cars in huge numbers.
  • A strict home market. Japan's inspection system and owners' habits mean cars are often traded in young, well maintained and with low mileage.
  • Auction grades. Japanese auctions grade every car, which gives Kenyan buyers and importers a degree of confidence about condition.
  • Toyota's reputation. Japanese cars, and Toyotas in particular, have a reputation for shrugging off bad roads and poor fuel, and parts are everywhere.

The eight-year rule

If there is one regulation every Kenyan car person knows, it is this one. Under the Kenya Bureau of Standards' standard KS 1515:2000, imported used vehicles may be no older than eight years from the year of first registration. In practice the cut-off moves every January 1st: from the start of 2026, KEBS will clear only right-hand-drive vehicles first registered in 2019 or later. That is why late 2025 brought a last-minute rush at Mombasa as importers tried to land 2018 cars before the deadline.

Vehicles from Japan also need a Certificate of Roadworthiness from KEBS's appointed inspection agent there, Quality Inspection Services Inc. Japan (QISJ). Without one, documents such as the logbook, export certificate and deregistration papers must be validated, which reportedly costs about KSh 12,000 per unit and takes around four days.

What the rule does to the scene

The eight-year limit has two big effects. First, it creates a rolling window: every year, a new generation of Japanese cars becomes importable and the oldest drops out. Second, it means classic JDM heroes such as the GC8 Impreza, old Skylines or the Mark II can only be found among cars already in the country, which keeps good examples precious. Newer, more powerful imports have also raised the performance bar at drag events.

The cars that rule our roads

CategoryKenyan favouritesWhy we love them
WorkhorseToyota Probox, SucceedCarries anything, costs little, never quits
City carToyota Vitz, Honda Fit, Mazda Demio, Nissan NoteCheap to run, easy to park, popular for ride-hailing
Family saloon or estateToyota Fielder, Axio, Premio, AllionPractical, comfortable, simple to fix
Crossover and SUVToyota Harrier, RAV4, Nissan X-Trail, Subaru Forester, Mazda CX-5Ground clearance for bad roads
StatusToyota Land Cruiser and PradoThe ultimate Kenyan statement
EnthusiastSubaru WRX and Legacy, Mitsubishi Evo, Toyota Mark X, Nissan SkylinePower, character and tuning potential

The Probox deserves special mention. It is so common that it has become a character in Kenyan life, carrying people, goods and occasionally an unbelievable quantity of both. Its rise was helped by its ability to carry passengers and cargo, although in 2019 the authorities banned its use, along with the Toyota Sienta, as a minibus because of overloading.

Modifying culture

Japanese cars arrive as a blank canvas, and Kenyans have never been shy with a spanner. The scene covers everything from tasteful wheels and lowered suspension to serious engine builds.

  • Wheels and stance. Aftermarket wheels are the first modification for most owners, though Kenyan roads punish very low profile tyres and slammed suspension.
  • Exhausts and intakes. The sound matters, especially for Subarus. Very loud exhausts invite attention from the police and the neighbours.
  • Turbo builds. Workshops in Nairobi now build engines for drag racing that rival anything in the region. Top Gear visited one Nairobi shop where a heavily built Subaru Impreza is estimated at around 900bhp.
  • Swaps and restorations. Engine swaps are common, and older icons are increasingly restored to standard rather than modified.
  • Wraps and lighting. Vinyl wraps, tints and lighting upgrades are popular, but stay within NTSA and insurance rules.

Where it all comes together

The JDM community meets on weekends at car parks, petrol stations and malls, and comes alive at organised events: time trials and gymkhanas, drag days on airstrips such as Masinga and Nyaribo, and track days at karting circuits such as Whistling Morans near Athi River. The Safari Rally weekend around Naivasha is the unofficial national JDM festival.

Buying a Japanese import: quick tips

  • Check the auction sheet and make sure the mileage and grade match the car in front of you.
  • Know the year of first registration, not just the model year, because it is what KEBS uses.
  • Budget for duty. Kenyan taxes are calculated using KRA's Current Retail Selling Price list, so a cheap car at auction can still cost a lot to clear.
  • Kenyanise it. Many imports benefit from a full service, new fluids and a careful look at suspension bushes before facing local roads.
  • Modify legally. Tell your insurer about modifications; an undeclared one can void your cover.
Japan built these cars. Kenya gave them character.

title: Car Spotting in Nairobi: Where to Find the Rare Stuff (and How to Behave)
excerpt: Nairobi hides more exotica than you would think, from vintage Rolls-Royces to rally legends. Here is where to look, when to go and the etiquette every spotter should follow.
content:
Nairobi is not Monaco. You will not see a queue of hypercars outside a casino on a Tuesday night. But the city is full of surprises for anyone who keeps their eyes open: a 1960s Mercedes being lovingly polished on a Karen driveway, an ex-works rally car resting on a trailer, a brand-new supercar in traffic on Waiyaki Way, crawling over a speed bump at walking pace with its nose lift raised.

Car spotting here is less about volume and more about the hunt. Here is how to do it well.

The big events: guaranteed treasure

The Africa Concours d'Elegance

The single best day of the year for spotting rare cars in Kenya. Held at Ngong Racecourse, usually in September or October, the Concours has been running since the early 1970s and gathers the finest classic cars and motorcycles in East Africa. The 54th edition, on 27 September 2026, was won by Veronica Duder's 1930 Essex Super Six, which tied on points with a 1930 Ford Tudor and took the title on a tiebreak because its marque was older. Other highlights included a 1925 Triumph motorcycle, a 1966 Mercedes-Benz 230 SL and an ex-works 1986 Nissan Silvia 200SX rally car.

Spotter's tip: arrive early, when cars are being driven in and prepared. That is when you see them move, hear them run and catch owners in the mood to chat.

The Safari Rally

The WRC Safari Rally Kenya, now based around Naivasha, is a feast for car people on and off the stages. Beyond the factory rally cars themselves, the spectator areas and roads around Naivasha fill with modified Subarus, Evos, Land Cruisers and the occasional properly exotic road car. The service park is a great place to see the works cars up close.

The Rhino Charge

If your taste runs to the bizarre, nothing beats the Rhino Charge. Spaceframe specials, giant tyres and twin winches: these are some of the most extreme off-roaders anywhere.

Track and drag days

Karting circuits such as Whistling Morans near Athi River and the TGRV track near Mai Mahiu host track days for road cars, and drag and gymkhana events are held at venues such as Masinga Dam Airstrip and Nyaribo Airstrip. This is where Kenya's fastest tuned cars come out to play.

Everyday hunting grounds

Away from events, rare cars tend to appear where money, good roads and parking meet. None of these is guaranteed, which is half the fun.

  • Upmarket malls on weekends. The car parks of the big malls in Westlands, Gigiri, Karen and along Thika Road and Limuru Road are reliable for luxury SUVs and the odd sports car.
  • Leafy suburbs. Karen, Runda, Muthaiga, Lavington and Kitisuru are where collectors live. You will see more on the way to church on a Sunday morning than at any other time.
  • Dealer showrooms. New-car showrooms and premium used-car yards often have halo cars on display. Always ask before you photograph inside.
  • Weekend coffee and car meets. Owners' clubs for Mercedes-Benz, BMW, Land Rover, Alfa Romeo, Subaru and others organise regular meets and drives, usually announced on social media.
  • The roads out of town. Early on Sunday mornings, convoys head for Naivasha, Magadi and Nanyuki. A petrol station on the way out of the city can be a goldmine.

What you are likely to see

CategoryTypical Nairobi findsRarity
ClassicsPeugeot 404 and 504, Mercedes saloons, early Land Rovers, VW Beetles, old Land CruisersOccasional; common at the Concours
Rally heroesSubaru Impreza, Mitsubishi Evo, old Celicas and NissansFrequent, especially around the Safari
Luxury SUVsRange Rover, G-Class, Land Cruiser 300, Lexus LXVery common in the right areas
Performance carsPorsche, AMG and M models, Audi RSWeekly if you know where to look
True supercarsLamborghini, Ferrari, McLarenGenuinely rare; a real prize

The holy grail, of course, is a car nobody expected: a JDM legend that slipped in years ago, a classic coming out of a barn after decades, or a supercar on its first drive in Kenya. Those are the photographs people talk about.

Spotting etiquette

Car spotting only works if owners feel happy to bring their cars out. A few rules keep it that way.

  • Look, do not touch. Never lean on, sit in or open a car without the owner's invitation. Bags, belts and buttons scratch paint.
  • Ask before close-ups. A quick "Do you mind if I take a few photos?" almost always gets a yes and often a conversation.
  • Be careful with number plates. If you post online, consider blurring plates and never share where a car is kept or when its owner comes and goes. Security matters here.
  • Never chase cars. Following a car through traffic for a photo is dangerous and illegal. Let it go; there will be another.
  • Do not ask for revs. Shouting "rev it!" at owners in public is how meets get banned. If they want to, they will.
  • Respect private property and security guards. If you are asked to leave a car park, leave politely.
  • Credit people. Credit photographers, owners (with permission) and event organisers when you share content.
  • Be kind about every car. The owner of a spotless Probox is as much a car person as the owner of a Lamborghini.

Kit for the serious spotter

  • A phone or camera with a decent zoom, so you can shoot from a respectful distance.
  • A notebook or app to log what you see; plenty of spotters keep year lists.
  • Patience. Some days you see nothing. Other days a convoy of classic Porsches turns up at your petrol station.
The best car spotters are the ones owners are glad to meet.

title: Best First Cars for Young Kenyan Drivers
excerpt: Cheap to buy, cheap to fix and kind to a new driver: the first cars we would recommend to a young Kenyan, plus what the eight-year rule means for your budget.
content:
Your first car is about freedom. It is also about learning, so it should be forgiving, cheap to run and inexpensive to repair when, not if, you misjudge a kerb in a Westlands car park. It is not the time for a turbocharged Subaru, however loudly your friends insist.

Here is our guide to choosing a first car in Kenya, with the models we would put at the top of the list.

What makes a good first car here

  • Cheap, available parts. In Kenya this usually means a popular Japanese model whose parts are sold on every street in Kirinyaga Road and in every town.
  • Simple mechanics. A naturally aspirated petrol engine is easier and cheaper to look after than a turbo or a complex hybrid.
  • Good fuel economy. Pump prices make this a big part of your running costs.
  • Safety kit. Look for multiple airbags, ABS and, on newer cars, stability control and autonomous emergency braking.
  • Sensible ground clearance. Enough to cope with speed bumps and potholes without scraping.
  • Low insurance costs. Small engines and common models are cheaper to insure, which matters a lot for new drivers.

The eight-year rule and your budget

From January 2026, KEBS only clears used imports first registered in 2019 or later. That means a fresh import will be relatively recent, with better safety equipment, but also more expensive and subject to higher duty. Older cars are still widely available locally used. For a first car, a well-maintained locally used example with full service history can be the smarter buy, as long as you have it inspected first.

Note too that some favourites changed names around that cut-off. The Toyota Vitz became the Yaris in Japan in 2020, the Mazda Demio became the Mazda2 in 2019, and both the Honda Fit and the Nissan Note moved to new generations in 2020. A "2020 Vitz" is really a Yaris, so search for both names.

Our top picks

Toyota Vitz / Yaris

The default answer, and for good reason. The Vitz is light, easy to drive, cheap to fix and simple to sell on. Engines range from a frugal 1.0-litre that suits town driving to a 1.3 and 1.5 that are better for highways and upcountry trips. A dealer guide puts typical Kenyan prices at roughly KSh 750,000 to KSh 1.3 million for 2015–2018 cars and KSh 1.4 million to 2.2 million for 2019-on models, depending on condition and mileage.

Check: CVT gearbox health on older cars, suspension wear and rust underneath.

Honda Fit

The cleverest small car on this list. The Fit's "magic seats" fold in ways that make it surprisingly practical, and it is roomier than it looks. Hybrids are common and very economical, but the hybrid battery and gearbox need checking carefully. Petrol versions are the simpler option.

Check: hybrid system warning lights, gearbox behaviour and the service record.

Mazda Demio / Mazda2

The driver's choice. The later Demio is the best-handling car here and feels well built inside. Petrol SkyActiv engines are economical; diesel versions exist but are best left to owners who know diesels.

Check: that parts and a mechanic who knows Mazdas are available near you. They are common, but not as universal as Toyota.

Nissan Note

Spacious, comfortable and good value. Many are e-Power versions, which use a petrol engine as a generator for an electric motor. They are smooth and frugal in traffic but more complex than a plain petrol car.

Suzuki Swift

Light, lively and fun, the Swift is the one that will make you smile on a winding road while staying cheap to run. It is a good choice if you want a little character.

Toyota Axio and Fielder

If you need more space, or the car will double as a family runabout, the Corolla-based Axio saloon and Fielder estate are almost indestructible and very easy to resell. They are slightly thirstier and more expensive to buy than the small hatchbacks.

ModelBest forWatch for
Toyota Vitz / YarisLow costs and easy resaleCVT on older cars
Honda FitPracticality, hybrid economyHybrid battery and gearbox
Mazda Demio / Mazda2Handling and qualityLocal specialist availability
Nissan NoteSpace and comforte-Power complexity
Suzuki SwiftFun on a budgetSmall boot
Toyota Axio / FielderSpace and toughnessHigher price and fuel use

What we would avoid for a first car

  • Turbocharged performance cars. Expensive to insure, expensive to fix and very easy to crash.
  • Big SUVs. They feel safe, but they are thirsty, harder to park and costly to maintain.
  • Rare European models. Lovely to drive, but parts can be slow to arrive and costly when they do.
  • Heavily modified cars. You inherit someone else's decisions, and insurers may not like them.

Buying checklist

  • Get a pre-purchase inspection from an independent mechanic you trust.
  • Verify the logbook and ownership through the NTSA's online system before paying anything.
  • For an import, check the auction sheet, the mileage and the year of first registration.
  • Test drive in traffic and over speed bumps, and listen for knocks from the suspension.
  • Budget for insurance, a full service, new tyres if needed and a set of fresh fluids straight away.
  • Never pay a deposit to someone you have not met for a car you have not seen.
The best first car is the one that teaches you to drive well and leaves enough money in your pocket to fill the tank.

A final word

Whatever you buy, invest in yourself as well as the car. A good driving school, an advanced or defensive driving course and a few hours practising in quiet car parks will do more for your safety than any feature list. The fun cars will still be there in a few years, and you will enjoy them more when you are ready.

title: Surviving Nairobi: How to Protect Your Suspension, Tyres and Clutch
excerpt: Crawling traffic, monster speed bumps and potholes that swallow rims: Nairobi is tough on cars. Here is how to keep yours healthy without living at the garage.
content:
Nairobi is a wonderful city in which to own a car, as long as you never actually want to drive it. Between the crawl on Mombasa Road, the speed bumps the size of small hills and the potholes that appear overnight after the first rains, our cars live a harder life than almost anywhere. A hidden pothole on Waiyaki Way once left a string of motorists with damaged rims and punctures in a single evening.

The good news is that most of the damage is avoidable. With a few habits and the right maintenance, your car can survive the city and your wallet can survive your mechanic.

Part one: suspension

Your suspension takes the hits so your spine does not. Shock absorbers, springs, bushes, ball joints, control arms and anti-roll bar links all wear faster on broken roads.

Driving habits that help

  • Look far ahead. The best way to deal with a pothole is to see it early. Leave a gap to the car in front so you are not driving blind into the hole it just swerved around.
  • Brake before, not in. Slow down before the pothole or speed bump, then release the brake as you go over. Braking hard compresses the front suspension and makes the impact worse.
  • One wheel, not two. If you cannot avoid a hole, it is better to put one wheel in it than both, and better still to go through straight rather than turning.
  • Take speed bumps slowly and squarely. Crawl over them at a slight angle only if your car is low enough to scrape the nose; otherwise hit them straight and slow.
  • Beware of puddles. In the rainy season a puddle can hide a deep hole. Treat standing water with suspicion.

Warning signs

  • Knocking or clunking over bumps, usually links, bushes or ball joints.
  • The car bouncing more than once after a bump, which points to tired shock absorbers.
  • Pulling to one side or a steering wheel that is no longer straight.
  • Uneven wear on the tyres.
  • Oil weeping from a shock absorber body.

Ask your mechanic to check the suspension at every service, not only when something sounds wrong. Replacing a worn link early is cheap; ignoring it can wear tyres and other components.

Part two: tyres and wheels

Tyres are the cheapest insurance you can buy against potholes.

  • Check pressures every week or two, when the tyres are cold, using the figures on the sticker inside the driver's door. An under-inflated tyre is far more likely to suffer a pinch cut or a damaged rim when it hits a sharp edge.
  • Do not go too low-profile. Big wheels with thin tyres look great at a car meet and terrible after a week on Ngong Road. A taller sidewall absorbs impacts and protects the rim.
  • Inspect sidewalls. A bulge or bubble means the internal structure is damaged. Replace the tyre; it can fail without warning.
  • Alignment and balancing. After a big hit, or if the steering feels off, have the alignment checked. Bad alignment can destroy a new set of tyres in months.
  • Rotate tyres at the intervals your handbook recommends to even out wear.
  • Look after the spare. Check its pressure too, and make sure the jack and wheel brace are in the car and that you have the locking wheel nut key if fitted.

Part three: the clutch and gearbox

Nairobi traffic is a clutch's worst nightmare. Hours of crawling, half-clutching up slopes and being stuck on the hill at a roundabout all add up.

For manual cars

  • Do not ride the clutch. Keep your left foot off the pedal unless you are using it. Even light pressure wears the release bearing and the friction plate.
  • Use neutral and the handbrake when you are stopped for more than a few seconds, instead of holding the car on the clutch.
  • Do not hold the car on a slope with the clutch. Use the handbrake for hill starts; it is what it is there for.
  • In slow traffic, use first gear and idle speed. Leave a gap and creep forward rather than repeatedly launching and stopping.
  • Know the signs. A biting point that rises higher and higher, a burning smell, or revs rising without the car speeding up all mean the clutch is wearing out.

For automatics and CVTs

  • Service the transmission fluid. Many Japanese imports use CVT gearboxes, which are sensitive to old or incorrect fluid. Use the specified fluid and change it at the recommended intervals, more often if you drive mostly in traffic.
  • Come to a complete stop before selecting reverse or park.
  • Do not rest your left foot on the brake. It heats the brakes and confuses the brake lights for the driver behind.

Part four: the underside, brakes and cooling

  • Fit a sump guard if your car is low. A cracked oil sump from a rock or a high speed bump is an expensive way to ruin a weekend.
  • Brakes work hard in stop-start traffic. Check pads and discs regularly and change brake fluid every couple of years, as recommended by the manufacturer.
  • Watch your temperature gauge. Sitting in traffic with no airflow tests the cooling system. Check the coolant level and make sure the radiator fan works.
  • Change your air filter more often. Dusty roads clog filters quickly, which costs power and economy.
  • Batteries suffer too. Short trips and long idling with the air conditioning on can drain a weak battery. Have it tested before the rainy season.

Part five: the rainy season

When the rains arrive, the roads change overnight. Water hides potholes, drains overflow and some roads flood completely.

  • Never drive into floodwater if you cannot see the road surface. If water enters the engine's air intake, it can wreck the engine instantly.
  • If you must go through water, go slowly and steadily to avoid a bow wave, then test your brakes gently afterwards to dry them.
  • Keep the wipers and tyres in good condition; aquaplaning is a real risk on worn tyres.
  • Switch on your headlights in heavy rain so others can see you.

A simple maintenance calendar

How oftenWhat to check
Every week or twoTyre pressures (including the spare), fluid levels, lights
Every monthTyre tread and sidewalls, wipers, a walk round for leaks
Every serviceSuspension, steering, brakes, CV boots, air filter
After a big impactRims, tyres, alignment and suspension
Before the rainsTyres, wipers, battery, brakes and lights

Insurance and paperwork

Read your policy. Some comprehensive covers pay for pothole damage to tyres, rims or suspension, others do not, and many have an excess that makes small claims pointless. Take photographs of the pothole and the damage at the time; they will help with any claim. Reporting dangerous potholes to the relevant road authority also helps the next driver.

The cheapest car repair in Nairobi is the pothole you saw coming.

None of this is glamorous, but it is the difference between a car that feels tight and quiet after five years and one that rattles over every bump. Treat your car with a little sympathy and it will look after you, through traffic, rain and every speed bump the city can throw at it.

title: Toyota Land Cruiser Prado 250 Review: The New King of the Kenyan Driveway
excerpt: The new Prado looks like a classic Land Cruiser and drives like a much more modern one. We find out whether it deserves its place as Kenya's favourite status symbol.
content:
Verdict at a glance

Toyota Land Cruiser Prado 250

Laqim score: 8.5/10

For

  • Superb off-road ability with locking diffs and a disconnecting front anti-roll bar
  • Strong, proven 2.8-litre turbodiesel with 500 Nm
  • Boxy retro styling that looks right in Kenya
  • Much better cabin, screens and safety kit than before
  • Toyota's reputation for durability and resale value

Against

  • Expensive to buy and to insure
  • Four-cylinder diesel is gruff and the performance is modest
  • Live rear axle makes the ride busy on broken tarmac
  • New body panels and lights are costly to replace

The Prado 250 is more capable, more modern and more desirable than ever, and for Kenyan roads it remains very hard to beat, if you can afford it.

A Prado for the Kenyan imagination

In Kenya, the Prado is more than a car. It is a promotion, a wedding convoy and a statement parked outside a county office. So when the 250-series arrived, the question was never whether Kenyans would want one. It was whether Toyota had kept what made the old one great.

The short answer is yes, and then some. CFAO Mobility Kenya officially introduced the new-generation Prado in July 2024, and since then it has become one of the most coveted vehicles in the country, whether bought new or imported from Japan, where it is sold as the Land Cruiser 250.

Design: back to the box

The 250 throws away the rounded, slightly anonymous look of the old Prado for a squared-off shape with a flat bonnet, upright windscreen and chunky wheel arches that recall Land Cruisers of the 1980s and 1990s. It looks tough because it is tough, and it photographs beautifully against red murram.

It is practical too. The lower beltline and reduced blind spots over the bonnet make it easier to place on narrow tracks, and the boxy body means good headroom and a big boot: 566 litres with five seats in use, according to UK testers. Seven-seat versions have a third row that folds flat into the floor.

Under the skin

The Prado now sits on Toyota's modern body-on-frame platform shared with the Land Cruiser 300, with a wheelbase stretched by 60 mm to 2,850 mm for better stability. Key hardware includes:

  • A 2.8-litre four-cylinder turbodiesel (the 1GD-FTV), producing about 201 hp and 500 Nm.
  • An eight-speed automatic replacing the old six-speed, which helps refinement and cruising economy.
  • Electric power steering, which also enables lane-keeping assistance.
  • A Stabiliser Disconnect Mechanism, which decouples the front anti-roll bar off-road to give the wheels more articulation.
  • Locking centre and rear differentials for serious terrain.

Some markets also offer a 2.7-litre petrol engine and a 48-volt mild-hybrid diesel, but the 2.8 diesel is the one most Kenyans will buy, and the one we would choose.

Key figuresPrado 250, 2.8 diesel
PowerAbout 201 hp
Torque500 Nm
Gearbox8-speed automatic, four-wheel drive
0–100 km/hAbout 11 seconds (UK test figure, 0–62 mph)
Wheelbase2,850 mm
Ground clearanceAbout 220 mm
Wading depthUp to 700 mm
TowingUp to 3,500 kg braked
Fuel tank80 litres

On Kenyan roads

On the tarmac out of Nairobi, the Prado is a big improvement on its predecessor. The ride is comfortable for a ladder-frame 4x4, even on large wheels, and the steering is accurate and well weighted. The eight-speed gearbox keeps revs low at cruising speeds, and wind noise is well controlled.

It is not perfect. The live rear axle can feel fidgety over the patchwork tarmac of a typical Kenyan highway, there is plenty of body roll if you hustle it through bends, and the four-cylinder diesel clatters when worked hard. Performance is adequate rather than exciting: it gets up the Rift Valley escarpment without complaint, but overtaking lorries on the Nakuru road takes planning.

Off the tarmac

This is where the Prado earns its badge. With high ground clearance, short overhangs, locking diffs and the front anti-roll bar disconnected, it climbs, crawls and wades with almost casual ease. A 700 mm wading depth is reassuring in the long rains, and the tough chassis copes with corrugated murram in a way that would shake a monocoque SUV to pieces. Safari guides and county surveyors will both approve.

Inside

The cabin is the biggest leap. Higher trims get a 12.3-inch touchscreen with Apple CarPlay and Android Auto, a digital instrument display, a head-up display, wireless charging and a premium sound system with up to 14 speakers. Toyota Safety Sense brings pre-collision braking, adaptive cruise control and automatic high beams. Some plastics on the centre console feel cheaper than the price suggests, and it is less plush than a Range Rover, but the layout is logical, with proper physical controls for the climate and four-wheel-drive systems.

Running costs

Economy is respectable for a two-tonne-plus 4x4. The official UK figure is 26.4 mpg (about 9.3 km per litre), and testers in the UK averaged around 24 mpg (about 8.5 km per litre). One Kenyan import specialist suggests 11–13 km per litre on the highway; expect less in Nairobi traffic. The 80-litre tank gives a decent range between fills, which matters upcountry.

The bigger cost is buying it. Estimates from a Kenyan import specialist put showroom prices at around KSh 13.5 million for a GX and about KSh 16 million for a VX or First Edition, with imports from Japan somewhat cheaper. Insurance is substantial, and the new body panels and lights are expensive to replace, so careful parking is a financial skill as well as a social one. On the plus side, Prados hold their value extremely well in Kenya.

What to watch

  • Body-on-frame means it will never ride like a car-based SUV.
  • Choose wheel and tyre sizes carefully; smaller wheels with taller tyres suit Kenyan roads better.
  • Use quality diesel and keep to service intervals; modern diesels with particulate filters dislike neglect.
  • Prados are a theft target; invest in tracking and good security.

The Laqim verdict

The Prado 250 is the best Prado yet. It is more capable off-road, much better on the road and far more desirable to look at than the car it replaces. It is not the most refined or the quickest SUV for the money, and a Land Rover Defender is the better car on smooth tarmac. But Kenya is not smooth tarmac. For a country where one vehicle has to do the school run, the upcountry funeral and the game drive, the Prado remains very close to perfect.

Expensive, a bit gruff and utterly unstoppable. Very Land Cruiser, in other words.

title: Subaru WRX Review: Can the New One Win Over Kenya's Subaru Faithful?
excerpt: The current WRX is quicker, smarter and more grown-up than any before it. But in a country raised on the EJ burble, is grown-up what we want?
content:
Verdict at a glance

Subaru WRX (VB generation, 2.4 turbo)

Laqim score: 7.5/10

For

  • Superb steering and an agile, grippy all-wheel-drive chassis
  • Strong, flexible 2.4-litre turbo engine
  • Comfortable enough for daily use, especially with adaptive dampers
  • Much better cabin and standard EyeSight safety tech
  • Instant credibility in Kenya's huge Subaru community

Against

  • Japanese-market cars, the most common imports, come only with a CVT-type automatic
  • Engine sounds flat compared with the old EJ burble
  • Low ground clearance needs care on Kenyan roads
  • Slow infotainment system and polarising black cladding

The current WRX is the most mature and usable WRX yet, but it has traded some of the drama that made Kenyans fall for Subaru in the first place.

The weight of history

No car arrives in Kenya with more baggage than a WRX. This is the badge that, thanks to the Safari Rally, the drag strip and a thousand Sunday meets, turned Subaru into a Kenyan cult. Every new WRX is measured against the GC8 and GD Imprezas that still rumble around Nairobi, and against the memories of Colin McRae and Richard Burns winning the Safari in blue and gold.

The current car, known to enthusiasts by its chassis code VB, launched in late 2021. It is no longer called an Impreza, it no longer has an EJ engine, and there is no STI version on sale. So is it still the car Kenyans dream about?

What it is

The WRX is a four-door saloon built in Gunma, Japan, on Subaru's latest platform. Power comes from a 2.4-litre turbocharged boxer four-cylinder, the FA24, driving all four wheels through Subaru's symmetrical all-wheel-drive system. How it is specified depends on where it was sold new, which matters a great deal in Kenya, because most WRXs here arrive used from Japan.

MarketNamePower and torqueGearbox
JapanWRX S4202 kW (275 PS), 375 NmSubaru Performance Transmission (CVT-type automatic) only
United StatesWRX271 hp, about 350 Nm6-speed manual or Subaru Performance Transmission

Japanese-market trims include the GT-H, GT-H EX, STI Sport R and STI Sport R EX, the last two with electronically adjustable dampers. In the United States the range runs from a base car to the sharper tS, which adds STI-tuned electronic dampers, Brembo brakes with six-piston front callipers and 19-inch wheels, and a limited-run Series.Yellow edition for 2026.

Under Kenya's eight-year import rule, every VB-generation WRX is currently eligible to be imported, which means the newest WRX is also the easiest one to bring in.

On the road

The first thing you notice is the steering. It is quick, precise and nicely weighted, with dual-pinion electric assistance, and it makes the WRX feel smaller and lighter than it is. Through a sequence of bends, such as the climb out of the Kerio Valley or the sweepers between Nyeri and Nanyuki, the chassis grips hard, turns in eagerly and puts its power down cleanly out of corners in a way that only a well-sorted all-wheel-drive car can.

The ride is also far better than old WRXs. In its softer settings, cars with adaptive dampers are genuinely comfortable for a performance saloon, and that matters when your daily commute includes Thika Road speed bumps. It still transmits more of the road surface than an ordinary saloon, but it never feels crashy.

The engine question

The 2.4-litre turbo is strong and tractable, with lots of mid-range torque that makes overtaking easy. Reviewers in the United States clocked 0–60 mph in around six seconds. It is effective, but it is not especially dramatic: the note is flat and there is little top-end rush. For a generation of Kenyans raised on the off-beat burble of the EJ engines, that is the biggest disappointment. You will not turn heads at a petrol station on sound alone.

The gearbox question

Most Kenyan WRXs will be Japanese WRX S4s, and those come only with the Subaru Performance Transmission, a CVT-type automatic with stepped "gears" and paddle shifters. It is smooth and efficient in Nairobi traffic, and far more usable than its reputation suggests, but it lacks the involvement of a manual. If you want three pedals, you will be looking for a rarer non-Japanese import.

Inside

The cabin is a huge step forward from earlier WRXs, with supportive sports seats, decent materials and a large portrait-style touchscreen. EyeSight driver assistance is standard. The weak point is the infotainment, which reviewers widely criticise as slow to respond, including with smartphone mirroring. Practicality is good for a sports saloon, with a usable rear seat and a proper boot.

The exterior is more divisive. The black plastic cladding around the wheel arches and sills is meant to evoke rallying, and from some angles it works. From others it looks unfinished, especially on lighter colours.

Living with one in Kenya

  • Ground clearance. Like every WRX, it sits low. Take speed bumps carefully, fit a sump guard and avoid the deepest potholes.
  • Fuel. Use the best quality super petrol you can find. Modern turbo engines are sensitive to fuel quality.
  • Servicing. Stick to frequent oil changes with the correct grade. Turbo boxer engines reward care and punish neglect.
  • Tyres. Performance tyres on 18- and 19-inch wheels wear quickly and can be damaged by potholes. Consider a set of tyres with a slightly taller sidewall for daily use.
  • Parts and expertise. Kenya has a deep pool of Subaru specialists, though they know the older EJ engines best. Choose a workshop with FA-series experience.
  • Insurance and security. WRXs are popular and attract attention. Shop around for cover and fit a tracker.

Rivals

In Kenya, the WRX's real rivals are other used Japanese performance cars: older Mitsubishi Lancer Evolutions (increasingly rare and expensive), the Toyota GR Yaris and GR Corolla for those who can find and afford them, and the Subaru Levorg estate, which shares much of the WRX's hardware in a more practical body. For many Kenyans, the WRX's biggest rival is an older, louder Impreza.

The Laqim verdict

Judged on its own, the current WRX is a very good car. It steers beautifully, grips tenaciously, rides well and is easy to live with every day, with a much nicer cabin and better safety kit than any WRX before it. It is the WRX you could recommend to someone who has to commute through Nairobi and still wants to enjoy the drive to Naivasha on Sunday.

But Kenya does not judge a WRX on its own. It judges it against legends. Without the sound, the rawness and, for most local buyers, the manual gearbox, this WRX feels more like a sophisticated sports saloon than a rally car for the road. It is the best-engineered WRX yet. It just is not the most exciting.

A brilliant all-weather sports saloon wearing a rally badge. Kenya's Subaru faithful will respect it, even if they do not quite love it.

title: Kenya's Most Iconic Cars of All Time
excerpt: The Peugeot 504, the Land Rover, the Hilux, the Probox and the humble Nissan matatu: the cars that built modern Kenya and still define how we move.
content:
Every country has its car. Italy has the Fiat 500, India the Ambassador, Cuba its American classics. Kenya has several, because no single vehicle could do everything this country asks of a car. We need saloons that survive murram, pickups that carry a harvest, 4x4s that cross rivers and minibuses that carry a city.

These are the cars that defined Kenya. Not necessarily the fastest or the most expensive, but the ones woven into our history, our roads and our memories.

Volkswagen Beetle

Start at the beginning. A Volkswagen Beetle won the very first Coronation Safari in 1953, driven by Alan Dix and Johnny Larsen, and Beetles won again in 1954, 1957 and 1962 (the last in a VW 1200). Its air-cooled engine could not boil over and its tough floorpan shrugged off the roughest roads. For a generation of Kenyans the Beetle was the first car in the family, and you will still find cherished examples at the Concours d'Elegance, where a 1968 Beetle won its class in 2026.

Peugeot 404

If one car marks the moment Kenya fell for the French, this is it. The Peugeot 404 won the Safari four times, in 1963, 1966, 1967 and 1968, with Nick Nowicki and Bert Shankland among its heroes. Its reputation for toughness made it a favourite of farmers, traders and families, and the 404 pickup became a rural workhorse that carried everything from milk churns to entire families. Elderly 404s are still lovingly kept running today.

Peugeot 504

The 504 was Kenya's signature saloon for a generation. Safari wins in 1975 and 1978 (the second in the V6 Coupé) proved its toughness, and its soft, long-travel suspension made it comfortable on roads that destroyed lesser cars. It was assembled locally for decades, with one report putting the number built in Kenya at roughly 27,000, and it served as a family car, a taxi, a company car and a fixture of official convoys.

The 504's decline came as it aged against more modern rivals: older cars developed a reputation for breakdowns, and it lacked the safety technology buyers came to expect. But ask any Kenyan over 40 about the 504 and watch them smile.

Land Rover Series and Defender

Few vehicles are as tied to the image of Kenya abroad as the Land Rover. From colonial farms and early safaris to research stations, missions and national parks, the Series Land Rovers and later the Defender went everywhere. They were simple, fixable with basic tools and tough enough for the roughest bush tracks.

Production of the original Defender ended at Solihull on 29 January 2016, after 68 years of the Land Rover line, but in Kenya they never really went away. Old Defenders are still working on farms and conservancies, restored ones are increasingly prized, and a 1999 Defender won its utility class at the 2026 Concours. The new Defender has become a common sight in Nairobi's wealthier suburbs.

Toyota Land Cruiser

If the Land Rover opened up the bush, the Land Cruiser took it over. Today the pop-top Land Cruiser 70-series is the default safari vehicle in Kenya's parks, and the bigger station wagons and Prados are the ultimate status symbols. A 1972 Land Cruiser FJ55 won its class at the 2026 Concours, proof that the old ones are now treasured classics. No other vehicle combines toughness, reliability and resale value quite like it, which is why the Land Cruiser remains the car every Kenyan aspires to.

Toyota Hilux

First launched in 1968, the Hilux is the backbone of rural Kenya. Farmers, contractors, county governments, NGOs and small businesses all rely on it. It carries produce to market, crews to building sites and equipment to places without roads. Its reputation for being almost impossible to kill is well earned, and a well-kept double-cab Hilux is one of the safest bets in the Kenyan used-car market.

The Nissan matatu

For decades, the 14-seater Nissan minibus was public transport in Kenya. So many Nissan vans worked as matatus in the 1980s and 1990s that "Nissan" became the generic word for a small matatu, and many Kenyans still use it today even though Toyota vans have long since taken over most of the fleet. The Nissan matatu carried millions of Kenyans to school, work and home every day, and laid the foundations for the colourful nganya culture that rules Nairobi's roads today.

Toyota Probox

The newest icon on our list, and perhaps the most Kenyan. Launched in Japan in 2002 as a humble delivery van, the Probox arrived here as a cheap used import and became something else: a taxi, a delivery truck, a farm vehicle and a rolling joke all at once. Kenyans tell endless stories about Probox drivers and the improbable loads they carry. It became so common as an informal passenger vehicle that in 2019 the authorities banned its use, along with the Toyota Sienta, as a minibus because of overloading.

It is not glamorous, but the Probox is honest, cheap to run and almost unbreakable. Few cars have done more for small businesses in Kenya.

Subaru Impreza

The enthusiast's icon. Safari wins in 1997 and 2000 for Colin McRae and Richard Burns, followed by regional victories for Kenyan drivers, made the blue-and-gold Impreza a hero. Cheap used imports turned it into a reachable dream for young Kenyans, and it built a culture of clubs, meets and drag races that continues today. The burble of an Impreza is one of the most recognisable sounds on Kenyan roads.

Mitsubishi Lancer Evolution

The Impreza's great rival deserves its place too. Mitsubishi's Safari history goes back to Joginder Singh's wins in the Lancer 1600 GSR in 1974 and 1976, and the Lancer Evolution then dominated the regional era, carrying Kenyan drivers to victory year after year between 2003 and 2019. The Impreza versus Evo debate is still the liveliest argument at any Kenyan car meet.

At a glance

CarKenyan claim to fame
Volkswagen BeetleWon the first Safari in 1953
Peugeot 404Four Safari wins and the rural workhorse pickup
Peugeot 504Kenya's signature saloon, assembled locally
Land RoverThe original bush and safari vehicle
Toyota Land CruiserToday's safari standard and status symbol
Toyota HiluxThe backbone of rural business
Nissan matatuGave its name to a generation of minibuses
Toyota ProboxThe unstoppable modern workhorse
Subaru ImprezaThe enthusiast's dream car
Mitsubishi Lancer EvolutionThe Safari's great regional champion
Kenya's iconic cars are not museum pieces. Most of them are still out there, working.

That is what makes this list special. Elsewhere, iconic cars are polished and parked. In Kenya, they still carry the harvest, the family and the morning commute. Which one is yours? Tell us, and tell us the story that goes with it.
